tour.title: Hillside Colour & Harbour: Gamcheon to Jagalchi
tour.summary: A hillside refugee village rebuilt as an open-air gallery, then a bus-and-metro hop round the hill to the old harbour: a wartime bazaar, the street a film festival made, Korea's biggest fish market, and the bridge where families searched for each other.
tour.overviewText:
Busan is the city South Korea fell back to. When North Korea invaded in June 1950, Seoul fell within days; Busan, in the south-east, was the only large city the North never took. The government moved here and stayed for 1,023 days, as wartime capital from 18 August 1950 until the armistice in 1953 — and the hillside village, the wartime markets and the bridge where families searched for each other are that war's southern legacy, walked in one afternoon.

Busan had been a port long before. It was the first Korean city opened to foreign trade, under a treaty with Japan in 1876, and the forty years of Japanese colonial rule from 1910 built it to serve the empire's shipping; the old commercial quarter around Nampo-dong still carries those bones. Today it is Korea's second city, about three million people, and its port is one of the ten busiest container ports on earth, moving more than twenty million TEU a year — a TEU, twenty-foot equivalent unit, being the standard shipping container.

The village where you start is the war's most human artefact. Refugees with nothing built up a slope nobody wanted, and a Korean new religious movement, the Taegeukdo, laid the houses out in tiers so no roof blocked a neighbour's light. Gamcheon peaked around 30,000 people in the 1980s, then emptied as the young left. In 2009 an art project painted the walls and filled abandoned houses with galleries, and by 2025 the village was drawing some 3.12 million visitors a year while its resident population had fallen below 6,000. Revival and displacement in the same lanes: that tension runs under the whole walk, and you will hear both sides of it.

Down at the harbour the subject turns to food and money. Jagalchi is Korea's largest seafood market, and its famous ajumma — the married and middle-aged women who run the stalls — took over the trade when the war left them widows, and never gave it back. Between the markets sits a street renamed for a film festival that began here in 1996 and grew into Asia's most important. Come in December and you are in crab season.

The shape is simple. You start high on the Gamcheon hillside and walk downhill through the lanes, then ride the bus and metro around the hill to the old harbour — barely two kilometres apart as the crow flies, far longer on foot — and spend the rest of the day on the flat, among the markets and quays.

Practicals, plainly. The route measures about 4.6 km and 55 minutes end to end, but roughly two-thirds of that is the long leg out of the village, ridden rather than walked. Entry to every stop is free; you pay for food, crab and the metro, at roughly 1,550 to 1,600 won a ride with a T-money or Cashbee card. Every price and hour here is approximate, so verify at the gate. Be at Gamcheon between 9am and 6pm, since the district restricts visitors on the residential lanes outside those hours, and note that a late-December sunset lands around half past five — a reason to start before lunch.

Come for the colour, stay for the argument about what a rescued neighbourhood owes the people who stayed.
tour.difficulty: Moderate, and honest about it. The Gamcheon half is relentlessly stepped and steep, all ups and downs on stone lanes with no wheelchair route to the viewpoints. The harbour half is flat, but the pavements and markets are crowded and the ground is wet around Jagalchi. Most of the distance between the two halves is ridden, not walked.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 10 or 11am in winter, or 1pm at other times of year. The residential lanes at Gamcheon are for visitors between 9am and 6pm only, so an early start also misses the worst queues at the Little Prince; you then reach Nampo-dong in daylight and finish at the bridge around dusk, when the harbour lights come on. In late December sunset is about 5:30pm, so an afternoon start means doing the markets in the dark. Jagalchi itself is liveliest early morning, when the boats land — if you want that, swap the order and finish at Gamcheon, which is legal but means climbing the hill in the afternoon.

stops.name: Gamcheon Culture Village Entrance
stops.narration:
You are standing on ground that people were pushed onto. Look up the hill: rows of small pastel houses stacked one above the other, each row set back so its roof does not steal the light from the row behind. In June 1950 North Korea invaded the South, and Seoul fell almost at once; Busan was the only large city the North never reached, so the government moved here and stayed for 1,023 days, the wartime capital from 18 August 1950 until the armistice in 1953. The city had about 280,000 people before the war; by the end it had more than 800,000. Flat land already belonged to people with money, so the refugees climbed and built on the bare slopes above town, where nobody charged rent. Koreans called hillside settlements like this daldongne, moon villages.

The Taegeukdo, the Way of the Great Ultimate, is a Korean new religious movement founded in the colonial era by Jo Cheol-je, called Jeongsan by his followers, and renamed Taegeukdo in 1950, the same year the war began. Its people moved here in numbers and set the houses out in disciplined tiers. Gamcheon itself means sweet water, after a spring on the hill. Most houses were under 33 square metres, built from wood, rock and corrugated iron.

Entry is free, because this is a neighbourhood, not a ticketed site; the information centre sells a stamp map for about 2,000 won that goes back to the village. Since 31 July 2026 Saha-gu district has run Gamcheon as an overtourism special management zone: visitors are kept to the marked routes, the residential lanes are for visitors between 9am and 6pm only, and groups of ten or more must buy a map. Roughly 5,600 people still live here, most of them elderly. Keep your voice down and stay on the orange-marked path.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the village; the visitor map with the stamp route costs about 2,000 ₩. Verify at the information centre, and note groups of ten or more are required to buy a map.
stops.openingHours: The lanes are open to visitors roughly 09:00 to 18:00: since 31 July 2026 the district restricts visitor access to residential streets outside those hours. The information centre keeps similar hours and can close earlier in winter. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free, bluntly. Gamcheon is stairs, ramps and steep stone lanes with no level route to the viewpoints, and the descent is hard on knees. Walkers with limited mobility can see the lower lanes and some of the view from the main road, but not the upper village.
stops.insiderTip: Before you climb, look at the rows from the side: each house sits back from the one below so every roof gets light. That stepped pattern was the Taegeukdo community's planning rule, and it is the reason the hillside photographs like a staircase instead of a shanty.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the information centre, take the orange-marked walking route uphill. It is signed and it is all steps — ten to fifteen minutes of climbing to the Haneul Maru viewpoint, the high platform over the village. If the stairs are too much, the upper stretch of the marked route still gives you most of the view.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Haneul Maru Observatory
stops.narration:
From up here you can see what the makeover bought. The terraces fall away toward Busan's South Port, container cranes standing in rows along the far quay, and on a cold clear day the water is hard and bright. This platform is Haneul Maru, meaning sky summit, and it is free, open roughly 9am to 6pm, the same hours you are allowed on the residential lanes.

Twenty years ago this was a dying neighbourhood. Gamcheon's population peaked around 30,000 in the 1980s and collapsed as young people left for the flat city; by the 2000s the district ranked near the bottom of Busan's own deprivation index, with empty houses and an ageing population. So the district tried art: from 2009, a village art project, run under names like Dreaming of Machu Picchu in Busan and followed by the Art Miro-Miro project in 2010, brought artists and students into empty houses, painted murals through the alleys, and turned abandoned rooms into galleries, workshops and cafés.

The numbers are the argument. Gamcheon drew about 3.12 million visitors in 2025, up from roughly 2.87 million in 2024 and 2.76 million the year before. In 2012 the village counted 9,677 residents; by the end of 2023 it had 5,668, a fall of more than 40 per cent in about a decade. Supporters point to a neighbourhood saved from abandonment, to work for residents, and to a district scheme that shares up to 30 per cent of the profits of local restaurants and souvenir shops with the people who live here. Critics call it gentrification with a paint job: noise, traffic, rubbish, lost privacy, and a community turned into a backdrop for other people's photographs. You can see both readings from this platform: on one side the queue at the statue below, on the other closed curtains.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free viewpoint. The village map and stamp route at the visitor centre cost about 2,000 ₩; verify at the desk.
stops.openingHours: Typically open about 09:00 to 18:00, in line with the district's visitor hours on the residential lanes. Confirm locally, and expect earlier closing in midwinter.
stops.accessibility: Reached by steps and steep ramps from the village entrance — not wheelchair accessible, and the last stretch is the steepest. There is no vehicle access to the platform itself.
stops.insiderTip: The cranes and the container port you can see from here are the same economy that pays for the flat city below — Busan moves more than twenty million shipping containers a year. Look for the harbour, then look down at the queue for the statue, and you have the whole argument of this village in one frame.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the platform on the marked route and follow the signs downhill toward the Little Prince statue — it is a few minutes of steps below you, and the queue is easy to spot. Do not retrace the way you came up; the route is a loop, and the downhill side takes you past the best of the murals.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: VaneTrz20, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Terraced Lanes & the Little Prince
stops.narration:
Meet the village's most photographed resident. That is the Little Prince, from Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's 1943 story, sitting on a wall with the Desert Fox beside him, both facing out over the rooftops. He arrived around 2013 as part of the village's art makeover. The classic photograph is taken from behind: sit beside him, look at the view rather than the camera, and step aside when you are done. The wait runs ten to thirty minutes at peak.

Now turn around and study the slope you just walked down. Gamcheon has almost no roads, only stairs, hairpin alleys and retaining walls. Water came from shared taps and waste went down shared drains. Houses stand shoulder to shoulder because every extra metre of frontage had to come out of a neighbour's window. The orange-paved path under your feet is an agreement to keep visitors on the official route, matched by the 9am to 6pm access rule brought in on 31 July 2026.

Busan is a city of exactly these hillside districts; the Korean term is sanbokdoro, mountain-road neighbourhood. In the 1960s and 70s the state bulldozed shanties and built rows of cheap hillside apartment blocks for the people it displaced. Gamcheon was redecorated instead of demolished, and even that brought friction: the village minibus is shared, and the district admits it fills with tourists before residents can board. The alleys are too narrow for a fire engine. The district's biggest fix is a road, widening a 1.5-kilometre approach from two lanes to four for 113.6 billion won, scheduled for 2028 to 2031. Then follow the lanes down to the main road, Gamnae 2-ro: the murals are painted on homes, so do not photograph through doorways or windows, or a face without asking.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. There is no ticket for the statue or the lanes — only the optional village map, about 2,000 ₩, sold at the visitor centre, and whatever you spend in the cafés. Verify prices locally.
stops.openingHours: The lanes are open to visitors about 09:00 to 18:00; outside those hours the district restricts tourist access to the residential streets. The statue is outdoors and always visible through the lanes, but the etiquette rule is the reason for the hours.
stops.accessibility: Continuous steps in both directions with only occasional handrails, and the descent is long. Not wheelchair accessible. The stairs can be slippery after rain or snow, which matters more than usual in winter.
stops.insiderTip: Skip the queue and shoot the statue from a few steps back with the rooftops behind it, then spend the time you saved on the alley below, where the murals are painted on private houses. Ask before photographing people — several residents also work as village guides and will happily tell you more.
stops.nextStopDirections: Follow the orange-marked lanes down to the main road, Gamnae 2-ro, where the buses stop. Keep to the marked route, keep your voice down, and remember the residential lanes are open to visitors from 9am to 6pm only; buses back into central Busan leave from the road below.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Christophe95, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Gukje Market
stops.narration:
You are in a market that exists because a war poured a country into one city. The name is the first clue: gukje means international. This began in 1945 on an empty lot as Dottaegi Market, dottaegi roughly meaning bustling, where people sold what departing Japanese colonists left behind. In 1948 it was renamed Jayu Market, Freedom Market, and in May 1950, a month before the Korean War began, it took the name it carries today.

Seoul fell, and by the end of 1950 some 200,000 evacuees from the capital had arrived in Busan; another 500,000 came south in January 1951, and 100,000 more crossed from the North after Chinese forces took Seoul. With the refugees came American soldiers, whose bases leaked goods Koreans were not supposed to own, let alone sell, so this market became the country's unofficial import shop and black market. It also burned: on 30 January 1953, three drunk cosmetics merchants knocked over an oil lamp in a market restaurant called Chunhyangwon. The fire burned for nine hours, destroyed around 1,600 structures and left 22,500 people from 6,800 households homeless.

What you see now is about 500 shops across a knot of covered alleys: the old import stores are closing, out-competed by the internet and cheap flights, while a younger generation moved in with vintage clothing and Japanese figurines. In 2014 a film named after the market, Gukje Market, released abroad as Ode to My Father, sold 14.2 million tickets, the fourth-biggest in Korean film history. Walk one block to Bupyeong Market and read its nickname: Kkangtong, which means tin can, earned when vendors sold American canned food during the war; its night market, one of the first in Korea, runs from about 7:30pm to midnight. Most shops open around 9am and close between 7pm and 8pm; some close one day a week, so verify at the shopfront.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. You pay only for what you buy; food-stall prices are posted and cash is still king in the older shops. Verify prices at the stall.
stops.openingHours: Most shops open around 09:00 and close between 19:00 and 20:00, and individual stalls set their own hours — many close one day a week. The neighbouring Bupyeong Kkangtong night market runs roughly 19:30 to midnight. Verify at the shopfront.
stops.accessibility: Mostly level but tight: narrow covered alleys, occasional steps and thresholds, goods stacked to head height, and heavy foot traffic. A wheelchair can manage the main aisles outside peak hours with a companion, but not the side lanes.
stops.insiderTip: Ask an older shopkeeper what they sold in the 1970s before you ask what they sell now — this market's whole history is who arrived from where, and the answers are usually a family's war story told in two sentences.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave Gukje Market by its southern side and follow the crowd into BIFF gwangjang-ro. BIFF Square is about 450 metres away, five or six minutes on foot; if you lose it, ask for BIFF gwangjang, and follow the smell of frying hotteok.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Ka23 13, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: BIFF Square
stops.narration:
You are standing in a street that renamed itself after a film festival. In August 1996 the district rebuilt this row of Nampo-dong and called it BIFF Square, and a month later, on 13 September 1996, the first Busan International Film Festival opened here with 169 films from 31 countries and 224 guests from 27, the first international film festival in Korea. Those were not small numbers for a country whose cinema had spent decades under government censorship: military governments had policed film content since the 1960s, and film-makers only got room to move after democracy arrived in 1987.

The festival grew into one of Asia's most important, and Korean film grew with it: in 2020 Bong Joon-ho's Parasite won the Academy Award for Best Picture, the first film not in English ever to do so. It gave this port city a claim to be where the country talks about film, which is part of why Busan campaigned to host the 2030 World Expo and lost the vote to Riyadh in November 2023.

Since 2011 the festival's main venue has been the Busan Cinema Center in Centum City, out east; this street is where it began, with handprints of Korean and foreign stars pressed into the pavement. Which brings us to the local dish. Hotteok is a Korean griddle cake: yeasted dough, flattened onto an oiled iron, filled with something sweet, folded into a hot pocket and pressed until the sugar melts. In Seoul the classic filling is brown sugar, cinnamon and crushed nuts; on this street you get ssiat hotteok, ssiat meaning seeds, stuffed with sunflower and pumpkin seeds and brown sugar, so it crunches as well as drips. It costs a few thousand won, there is usually a queue at the stalls that have been on television; check any price at the counter.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free — it is a public street. Street food such as ssiat hotteok runs a few thousand won per piece; verify the price at each stall, especially at the stalls with the longest queues.
stops.openingHours: The street is public and open at all hours; the food stalls and shops generally run from late morning into the evening, later on weekends. Individual stalls set their own hours, so verify on the day.
stops.accessibility: The most accessible stop on the walk so far: a paved, level pedestrian street, step-free throughout, with the usual caveat that it gets very crowded in the evening and around festival time.
stops.insiderTip: Read the pavement as you walk: the handprints and signatures set into the stone are the festival's own archive of who came through Nampo-dong in the early years. Then look for the stage at the far end of the alley, where the festival still holds events in its old heartland.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south-west out of BIFF Square toward the water, about 300 metres and four minutes. Cross the main road, Gudeok-ro, at the lights and head for the harbour — the market building with the fish on the sign, and the outdoor stalls in front of it, are Jagalchi.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: cezzie901, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Jagalchi Fish Market
stops.narration:
Jagalchi comes from jagal, gravel, the pebbles that covered this shore before anyone sold anything on it. Today it is the largest seafood market in South Korea: a building with tanks and stalls downstairs and restaurants above, an open-air row of vendors on the quay, and a business run mostly by women. Ask who the Jagalchi ajumma are and you are asking about the Korean War. Ajumma is the ordinary Korean word for a married or middle-aged woman, and here it is a job title. When the fighting emptied the fishing villages of men and filled Busan with widows and refugees, women took over the trade, and they never handed it back. The ajumma are stallholders and bosses, so buy from them, ask the price before you point, and ask before you photograph anyone's face.

Downstairs is the wet market: tanks of flatfish and octopus, crabs lined up on ice. You choose, negotiate and pay by weight. Then someone cooks it, either in the upstairs restaurants or in one of the small places that will prepare your purchase for a cooking charge, usually around 10,000 won for the table plus side dishes. Hoe is the Korean word for raw fish. Verify every charge at the stall before you commit.

December is the right month for crab. Snow crab, daege, comes from Korea's cold eastern waters, where the season opens in late November and runs into spring. King crab, kingkeuraep, is in most Korean markets an import, largely from Russia and Alaska. Prices move with the day's landings: expect roughly 50,000 to 75,000 won per kilogram, more for a large king crab, and treat any figure as today's. The market runs from about 5am to 10pm and closes on the first and third Tuesday of each month. In autumn it holds its own festival, whose slogan says everything: Oiso! Boiso! Saiso! Come! See! Buy!
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; you pay per weight for seafood, plus a cooking or table charge at the restaurant — around 10,000 ₩ for the table, verified at the stall. Crab runs roughly 50,000–75,000 ₩ per kilogram in winter and moves daily.
stops.openingHours: Generally about 05:00 to 22:00, and closed on the first and third Tuesday of each month. Individual stalls vary, and the catch is liveliest early morning. Verify before planning around it.
stops.accessibility: The main building has ramps and lifts to the upstairs restaurants, but the ground floor is wet, sloped, crowded and loud, with hoses and crates underfoot. The outdoor stalls are on level quay. Take the floor seriously — fish water on tile is slick.
stops.insiderTip: Buy downstairs, eat upstairs: pick your fish or crab at the tank, agree the price and the cooking charge, then take the receipt to one of the upper-floor restaurants. And note the market's own slogan for its autumn festival — Oiso! Boiso! Saiso!, come, see, buy — because that, for a century, has been the whole business model.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the market on the harbour side and walk east along the waterfront, keeping the water on your right. Yeongdo Bridge is about 600 metres away, eight to ten minutes on foot, and the steel lifting span is obvious ahead of you; cross the road carefully and finish on the bridge itself.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Doo Ho Kim, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Yeongdo Bridge
stops.narration:
Here is where the walk ends, on the bridge that carried the war's grief. Yeongdo Bridge was completed in 1934, when Korea was a colony of Japan, to link the mainland to Yeongdo island across the mouth of Busan's south port. It was Korea's first drawbridge, a bascule bridge, a span that lifts on a counterweight so that ships can pass. With hundreds of thousands of refugees packed into Busan and families split across the peninsula by the front line, this bridge became the place you came to look for someone. It is remembered as the bridge of reunions, and, because far more people searched than found, as a bridge of tears as well.

The lifting machinery broke down in 1966, and by 2003 the bridge was close to demolition. Instead it was preserved, restored and reopened on 27 November 2013 with the drawbridge working again: most Saturdays the span lifts at 2pm for about fifteen minutes, and in summer there are night lifts around 8pm. Maintenance has paused the show at times.

Now look back at what you crossed. Up on the hillside, a village of refugees who arrived with nothing and laid their houses out so that no neighbour lost the light. Down in the markets, a wartime import bazaar that became a national memory, and a fish market where women turned a war that widowed them into a trade they owned outright. And the port underneath all of it: Busan moves more than twenty million containers a year, and that traffic built the bright, flat city you walked through. Across town, in the only United Nations cemetery in the world, 2,300 soldiers from eleven countries are buried. If it is winter and your wallet can bear it, a crab is waiting back at Jagalchi; if not, take a coffee and watch the harbour lights come on over Yeongdo.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free — it is a working public bridge. No ticket for the bridge or for watching the drawbridge lift; only whatever you spend on the Nampo-dong side after.
stops.openingHours: The bridge is open to traffic and pedestrians at all hours. The drawbridge lift is usually on Saturdays at 14:00 for about fifteen minutes, with additional night lifts around 20:00 on summer weekends; the mechanism has been taken out of service for maintenance at times, so verify locally before you plan around it.
stops.accessibility: Level, paved pavement onto and across the bridge, step-free, with a slight rise over the span. The lift event draws a crowd along the quay, which is the only real obstacle.
stops.insiderTip: Stand at the middle of the span at dusk, with the fish market behind you and the container cranes up the harbour ahead — the two halves of this walk in one view. Nampo and Jagalchi metro stations are both about five minutes' walk back, so the way home is easy wherever you are staying.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Both Nampo and Jagalchi stations on Metro Line 1 are a five-minute walk back into the market district, and taxis line the Nampo-dong streets. If you have time left, the food alleys behind BIFF Square keep going late; if it is Saturday and the lift is running, stay for the 2pm show on the bridge.
